How to play

1 Observe Study the desk scene before the screen briefly goes blank.
2 Find the change When the scene returns, click the changed object—or the spot where it was.
3 Try another set Play again to see a different mix of changes.

Why this game

What change blindness teaches us about interface design

I came to HCI from neuroscience, and I wanted this game to make that connection visible. Change blindness is a phenomenon related to perception, attention, and memory: even when something is directly in front of us, the brain may fail to register that it changed—especially when the scene is briefly interrupted.

That same limitation matters in HCI because interfaces are constantly changing. A form saves, a system status updates, an error appears, a permission changes, or new information arrives. Simply placing that change on the screen does not guarantee that the user will notice or understand it. Contrast, movement, placement, timing, and feedback all influence whether a change actually reaches attention.

I made this a game because reading about change blindness is very different from experiencing it yourself. Missing a change that was visible the entire time makes the idea immediate—and turns an abstract neuroscience concept into a practical design lesson.

The variations are intentionally mixed. An object might move, rotate, change color, flip direction, switch state, or disappear. This keeps the player from learning one predictable pattern and shows that attention can miss many different kinds of visual information.

This is a playful demonstration, not a scientific assessment of attention or memory. It is one example of how I connect neuroscience and HCI; the other games explore different ideas from perception and cognition through interaction.
